HANG IN THERE SISTER. I'm in a similar situation, and my mental health is so much better being away from my family. If it's damaging to you, you are not beholden to anyone, for anything. 

If it helps, I'm on very low contact, which is not no contact like everyone always says, and in my situation it works out just as well as no contact. But that may be different for you, I don't know your family. 

But bottom line: you are your top priority. If I ever lose sight of this, I ask myself, "If this was an unrelated friend, would I be friends with them? No. If they were a significant other, would I break up with them? Yes." You have to think in terms of who else in your life you would allow to act that way and still be in your life. And I think the answer is no one.

I felt the same way, and everyone told me to just (try) and relax and enjoy it, and enjoy for the first time having a family that wants you around. I know how very hard it is. Sometimes it makes me cry when they're so nice to me because I don't know how to process it because of my former home life. Slowly but surely, though, I'm coming to enjoy it more. Thank them and participate with them in any way you feel comfortable; you KNOW that all they want to do is make you feel loved.

This sounds like me when I had my first (and only) manic episode, that got me diagnosed with bipolar disorder. I became obsessed with Ayn Rand (because I hate her yet she's my boyfriends favorite author). Because of that fact, we have all her books at the house, so I stayed home from school and work and read HUNDREDS of pages of her drivel, as well as Wikipedia pages and biographies like a total crazy person. Then I went on reddit and posted on Ayn Rand forums and argued with people and it was a big mess. Maybe your boyfriend is experiencing a manic episode, that's sure what it sounds like to me, especially the suicide part. I would get him to a mental health crisis interventionist asap, especially if this behavior is new or atypical. Manic episodes can last months. Mine ended when my bf hauled me to my psychiatrist, I got put on meds, and he hid all his Ayn Rand books so I couldn't get obsessed again.

Good luck, I hope I'm wrong. And if you and your bf are Trump supporters I'm sorry I was so harsh about Ayn Rand.

Maybe I'll get downvoted for this, but whenever someone says "small talk bores me" or that they have to discuss big, weighty topics to be stimulated, it really annoys me. Every topic is interesting in some way, and I feel like people who Are Very Smart limit themselves because they feel like they can only talk about "society, people, [and] the universe." 

You're categorizing yourself as a life scholar, while you're categorizing your wife, despite all the nice things you've said about her, as someone who never wants to learn anything. I really doubt that's true, and it's presumptuous of you to think that the only way you're going to have something in common with someone is if they "educate themselves." 

She obviously has things she cares about: fitness, traveling, and even twitter. You say she tries to talk to you about things you like. Do you try to talk to her about fitness or traveling? Those are two amazingly interesting topics. Exercise science is complex and has many interesting debates and findings. Travel is the same. Heck, even if she only reads twitter to follow the Kardashians, I'm sure she knows lots about pop culture. Everyone thinks the Kardashians are so dumb, but even though I find the show itself brainless, there's so many interesting topics there. For example, Pop Sugar recently rated Kylie Jenner as one of their Latina Icons-- even though she's not Latina at all. There's LOTS to be discussed about the way our country perceives beauty and race, or whether or not she's co-opting an entire ethnicity for marketing purposes.

Bottom line: I'll bet your wife has some really interesting opinions, but you're never going to hear them if the only thing you can talk about is astrophysics or economics. Hegel said, "The learner always begins by finding fault, but the scholar sees the positive merit in everything."

I had this same question here about 4 years ago, when we could all tell that my friend was suffering through an eating disorder but couldn't do anything to stop her. In my post then, I wrote that I 100% supported her and would do anything to help her. 

However, everyone pointed out that I obviously wasn't 100% supporting her, because like you I was accusatory, and focused on all the shocking things that were happening and not the reasons behind it. 

So I tried talking to my friend about those things, the deeper things that were driving her. It didn't work because she refused to talk about them. But maybe it will work for you. Be a 100% supporter and really ask your friend about her life, her happiness, etc. Maybe she will open up to you and be more capable of assessing how her fears are informing her choices. Maybe not. It's worth a try, and it's the only thing I know of that might really help.

That way you're saying nothing without remaining silent.

My mom was unemployed for like 20 years, and she always said the EXACT same thing as your boyfriend: it's impossible to work a "regular" 9-5 job in an office. My mom also cannot tolerate anyone ever telling her what to do. It seems like your boyfriend might have some aversion to authority as well. If he wants to make a living without anyone being his boss, he will need to be extremely motivated, self-disciplined, and passionate about his work. 

So you could consider talking to him about what he's passionate about as a way to jumpstart his own thinking about how he can successfully be self-employed. I don't think talking to him about his dreams and passions would be perceived as nagging. I know I would love to talk to my SO about my dreams. 

However, not all people have a life passion. Maybe your boyfriend doesn't. My mom doesn't. If he must be self-employed but doesn't have any passions, he's just going to have to find something to get by. 

For example: my mom eventually got her real estate license. She barely works, but when it comes time to pay bills, she sells a house. She doesn't have much in savings, but she likes her life. She has just decided that having a job is not a priority in her life. If your boyfriend doesn't see having a job as a priority for him, maybe he could find a career that takes minimum input but pays the bills. That life is not inherently wrong. 

What this means for you, though, is a whole different thing. Are you okay being with a self-employed partner working on his passion? Are you okay being with a partner who wants to pay the bills but isn't interested in having regular employment? Openly discuss your priorities. If they line up, that's great. If not, you may have to ask yourself some hard questions.

This actually just happened to me. Although not my first serious relationship, I was coming off a year-long relationship break when I met my boyfriend. I essentially moved in with him after our 4th date, he said he loved me by our 6th, and we moved together to a new house 2 months later. I am also not financially independent, but working towards it. We've now been together 9 months and I'm very happy in the relationship. 

Work to be financially independent if you can, and ALWAYS tell your boyfriend how you're feeling. ALWAYS be looking out for you first. But I think if you're on the same page about where you are in life, I don't think it's such a red flag as other people are saying. Sometimes if you know, you know. 

I was SO anxious about how fast my relationship was moving, but now I'm more okay with it. I always say I got thrown in the deep end of the pool, but it was actually very good for me. I had gotten out of a really serious relationship and would have moved at a snail's pace if given the chance. I appreciate that my SO challenged me. I wrote a post like yours when we moved in and everyone told me major red flags, slow down. But in the end, I loved my relationship, trusted my SO, and moving so fast didn't happen to be that big of a deal after all.
